title: A wrong accent, a backwards name
hookLine: a word said wrong, Tvashtr's misplaced accent, and the robber who said Rama's name backwards
carry: vedic chant guards each sound; the name wants the heart
tomorrow: why would a poor singer turn down a king's gold?
last: THE SEAT IS FOR THE LISTENER.

cards: A wedding toast, a name read at graduation, a line said at a family puja: someone gets a word wrong, and the room splits. Half wince. Half say, relax, they meant well.
Hindu tradition has this argument too, with a story for each side. Here's the first. Tvashtr, a craftsman god, wants a son who will kill Indra.
He pours the offering and calls out the son's name: indrashatru. But he puts the accent in the wrong place. Said one way, the word means slayer of Indra.
Said his way, it means the one whose slayer is Indra. And that is how the story ends.

teach.h: A WRONG SOUND SAYS THE WRONG THING.
teach.b: The Paniniya Shiksha, an old manual on sounds, turns that story into a warning.
A mantra said with a wrong sound or a wrong accent doesn't say what it means, and can even turn on the one who says it, the way indrashatru did.
On this side stands Vedic chant, whose chanters give years to getting every syllable and accent right. Their best case: these words were handed down by ear, one mouth to the next.
Small carelessness, repeated over generations, would wear a verse away. Exactness is a form of care. Now the other story.
In a telling found in the Adhyatma Ramayana, a robber who will one day be the sage Valmiki can't bring himself to say Rama's name. So sages give it to him backwards: mara, mara.
Said over and over, mara mara runs together into rama rama. Tradition says he repeated it until an anthill grew over him.

teach.h: NAMA JAPA: A WHOLE HEART IS HEARD.
teach.b: On this side stands nama japa, repeating the name of God, one of the most common Hindu practices there is, said with love, accent or no accent.
Their best case: God isn't fooled by a mouth, and a name said with a whole heart reaches where it's meant to go.
The tradition holds both. Vedic chanters keep the first for the Vedas. Bhakti, the way of loving devotion, keeps the second for the name.
And some keep both at once: care with the sound, and the heart behind it.

how: Vedic chanters train for years to keep every syllable and accent exact, while bhakti traditions sing and repeat the names of God in many accents and languages; some families hold both in the same home.

o: Sanskrit's sounds, which some say must be exact
Sanskrit's rhythms, which must be sung loudly
Sanskrit's letters, which must be written neatly

games.q: two stories, two sides — tap the pairs.
p: a name that flipped with its accent
wanted a son to slay Indra

s: in the story, Tvashtr's mistake was saying the wrong word
the word was right. the accent was wrong, and the meaning flipped.
in the Adhyatma Ramayana's telling, the robber first says the name backwards
mara, mara, which runs together into rama, rama.
Hindu tradition says pronunciation never matters as long as you mean it
the Shiksha guards every sound; bhakti stresses the heart. both views live inside the tradition.

games.q: at a family puja your uncle says a line of Sanskrit with the accents all over the place. you lean toward the heart side. what's the best case for the other side?
o: words handed down by ear would wear away if no one guarded each sound.
God hears only perfect Sanskrit, so the whole puja doesn't count now.
correcting an elder out loud is a duty, wherever you are.
games.why: the chanters' case is care: the Shiksha warns a wrong sound can say the wrong thing, as indrashatru did. a fair steelman keeps that case at its strongest, not its harshest.

practice: If you pray, choose one name of God you love, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Devi, and say it slowly, eleven times, as japa: each sound with care, and the heart behind it.
If you don't pray, write one name you love by hand, every letter where it belongs, then read it once with that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: today, two old answers to whether they must be exact. Vedic chant's care, and the devotee's heart in nama japa.

orig.note: Sanskrit: indraśatru. Accented one way, slayer of Indra; the other way, the one whose slayer is Indra.

carryVoice: For the road: vedic chant guards each sound; the name wants the heart. Hinduism keeps both. That's today.

sources.ref: Shatapatha Brahmana 1.6.3.8–10 (Tvashtr's offering, indrashatru said with the wrong accent)
Paniniya Shiksha 52 (a mantra faulty in accent or letter does not convey its meaning; the word becomes a thunderbolt, as indrashatru did)
Adhyatma Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 6 (Valmiki given the name as mara; the anthill)
